passages.passage_text:
Kant's claim that only actions done from duty have moral worth strikes many readers as cold. The shopkeeper who gives correct change because honesty is good for business acts in accordance with duty, Kant says, but not from duty; his action would vanish the moment cheating became profitable and safe. Even the sympathetic person who delights in helping others, Kant continues, deserves praise and encouragement but not esteem in the strict sense, because inclination is a fortunate accident of temperament rather than an achievement of the will. Critics have heard in this a demand that we suppress affection, and Schiller's quip that Kant would have us help our friends with a sigh of reluctance has become the standard summary of the objection.

The objection, however, misreads what Kant is isolating. He is not recommending that we cultivate reluctance; he is asking what, in a good action, makes it good. His answer is that the worth lies in the principle on which the agent acts, not in the outcome and not in the feeling that accompanies it. A person moved by pity who helps a stranger has done something admirable in its effects, but if we ask whether she would have helped when pity failed, we learn whether her conduct was governed by a principle or merely by a mood. Kant's famous thought experiment of the person whose sympathy has been extinguished by grief, who nevertheless helps others purely because it is right, is a test device. It strips away the motive that normally accompanies helping so that the contribution of duty can be seen alone, as one isolates a single variable in an experiment. It does not follow that a life without inclination is the ideal.

What, then, does duty require? Kant's categorical imperative asks whether the maxim of one's action could be willed as a universal law. A maxim of making false promises to escape difficulty fails, since if everyone adopted it the practice of promising would collapse and the maxim would defeat itself. This procedure is often presented as a mechanical decision rule, and as such it generates well-known embarrassments: maxims can be described so narrowly that almost anything passes, or so broadly that harmless actions fail. Defenders reply that the imperative is better read as a constraint on deliberation than as an algorithm. It does not tell us what to do; it screens out proposals that make an exception of ourselves, that claim for our own case a license we would not extend to anyone else.

Seen this way, Kantian duty is less a rival to compassion than a safeguard against its unreliability. Compassion is selective: we feel more for the one child in a well than for thousands in a famine, more for those who resemble us than for strangers. A morality grounded in feeling inherits these biases. Duty, by contrast, binds us equally toward persons whom we do not love and cannot see. The price is that Kant's ethics seems to leave little room for moral luck, for the way outcomes and temperament shape how we are judged. A will that is good even if wholly lacking power to accomplish its purpose shines, he says, like a jewel for its own sake. Whether that picture is noble or evasive remains the central dispute between Kant and his critics, and perhaps it is a dispute about whether morality is chiefly about who we are or about what we bring about in the world.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Kant held that acting from compassion is morally worthless, and the passage endorses this view because feelings are always unreliable guides.
options.B: Kant's emphasis on duty is a claim about where moral worth lies, and it can be defended against the charge of demanding emotional coldness.
options.C: Kant's categorical imperative is a mechanical decision procedure that settles every moral question without any need for judgment from the agent.
options.D: Kant's ethics succeeds because it gives outcomes and temperament the central place in how we should evaluate individual moral agents.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the passage defends duty-based worth against the coldness objection while noting a remaining dispute. Why the others are wrong: A) Kant says sympathy deserves praise; the passage says it is merely not what confers strict worth, and it never calls feelings worthless. C) The passage says the imperative is better read as a constraint than as an algorithm. D) Kant locates worth in the principle of the will, and the passage says his ethics leaves little room for outcomes and luck.
questions.trap: Choosing the extreme version of Kant's view (feelings are worthless) instead of the passage's more qualified claim that inclination is not the source of strict moral worth.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the thought experiment of the person whose sympathy has been extinguished by grief is intended to

options.A: recommend that moral agents try to cultivate emotional detachment so that their helping behavior becomes more reliably principled over time.
options.B: show that people who are grieving are exempt from the ordinary demands of the categorical imperative toward strangers in need.
options.C: isolate the contribution of duty by removing the motive that usually accompanies helping, much as an experiment isolates a single variable.
options.D: demonstrate that sympathy and duty always produce conflicting recommendations, so that one of them must be abandoned in practice.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the passage calls the case a test device that strips away inclination so duty can be seen alone. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says explicitly that it does not follow that a life without inclination is ideal. B) Nothing in the passage suggests an exemption; the person in the example helps anyway. D) The passage argues duty and compassion need not be rivals, and often coincide.
questions.trap: Reading a diagnostic thought experiment as a recommendation for how people should live.

questions.stem: The shopkeeper example is used in the passage to illustrate an action that is

options.A: in accordance with duty but not from duty, because its motive would disappear if cheating became safe and profitable.
options.B: from duty and also from inclination, because the shopkeeper's honesty is both principled and pleasurable to him in each transaction.
options.C: contrary to duty but beneficial, because the shopkeeper's concern with profit corrupts what would otherwise be a perfectly neutral act.
options.D: from duty but morally unremarkable, because giving correct change is such a trivial act that no moral worth could attach to it.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) correct change given only because honesty pays matches duty in outward result but not in motive. Why the others are wrong: B) The shopkeeper is moved by profit, not by duty, so the action is not from duty. C) The act itself is what duty requires; the problem lies in the motive, not the act. D) Triviality is not the issue; the issue is the motive behind the action.
questions.trap: Confusing the outward conformity of an action with duty with the agent's motive for performing it.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most undermine the defenders' reading of the categorical imperative as a constraint rather than an algorithm?

options.A: Most people who apply the test to their own proposed actions reach different verdicts than their friends reach about the same proposals, even after discussing them at length.
options.B: The universalization test rules out some proposals, such as false promising, that many people already regard as wrong for other reasons.
options.C: Kant himself sometimes disagreed with later interpreters about how to describe maxims in applying the imperative to specific cases.
options.D: Applying the universalization test to any situation always yields exactly one permissible action, whatever description of the maxim is chosen.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) if the test always produced a unique answer regardless of description, it would function as a decision algorithm, contradicting the defenders' reading. Why the others are wrong: A) Disagreement in verdicts is consistent with a constraint that does not fix a single answer. B) Screening out some proposals is exactly what a constraint on deliberation does. C) Interpretive disagreement does not show the test is an algorithm; it fits the constraint reading.
questions.trap: Treating any fact about disagreement as damaging, rather than asking which fact would show the procedure is mechanical.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a Kantian would most likely criticize a charity that distributes aid solely according to which appeals stir donors' strongest feelings because such a policy

options.A: treats recipients as means to the donors' pleasure, which the passage identifies as the sole ground of Kant's concern with charity.
options.B: inherits the selectivity of compassion, favoring those who resemble us or are vividly presented over others in equal need.
options.C: fails to calculate the total amount of welfare produced, which the passage describes as the chief test of a morally good action.
options.D: relies on universal laws that cannot be willed without contradiction, as in the example of the false promise to escape difficulty.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the passage says compassion is selective and a morality grounded in feeling inherits those biases, whereas duty binds equally. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage never says that using persons as means is the sole ground of the concern; it focuses on selectivity. C) The passage rejects outcomes as the source of worth, so welfare totals are not Kant's test. D) The false-promise example concerns self-defeating maxims, not the biases of feeling-driven aid.
questions.trap: Importing a different Kantian doctrine from outside the passage instead of using the passage's own argument about compassion's selectivity.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage serves mainly to

options.A: conclude that Kant's critics are mistaken because moral luck has no genuine influence on how people are judged by others.
options.B: restate the claim that duty is a safeguard against the unreliability of compassion in the cases of strangers and friends alike.
options.C: frame the unresolved dispute between Kant and his critics as a question about whether morality concerns character or consequences.
options.D: propose a compromise in which actions are judged by their outcomes when sympathy is present and by principle when it is absent.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) it raises the broader issue, who we are versus what we bring about, that underlies the disagreement. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says the ethics leaves little room for moral luck, and it does not argue moral luck is illusory. B) That safeguard point was made earlier; the last sentence moves to the larger dispute. D) No compromise is offered; the passage ends by leaving the dispute open.
questions.trap: Mistaking a closing reflection that leaves a question open for a conclusion that settles it.

passages.passage_text:
Since Gibbon, the fall of the Roman Empire has served as a mirror in which each age sees its own anxieties. Gibbon, writing in the Enlightenment, blamed the loss of civic virtue and the rise of Christianity, which he thought redirected loyalty from the state to the afterlife. Nineteenth-century nationalists preferred racial and migratory explanations, picturing a vigorous Germanic north overwhelming a tired Mediterranean south. Twentieth-century scholars, living through world wars and economic crises, pointed to fiscal strain, inflation, and the burdens of a vast military. That the same events could support such varied narratives should make us cautious, but it has not stopped historians from continuing to look for a master explanation.

The most influential recent revision is the idea of late antiquity, associated with Peter Brown, which treats the centuries between roughly 250 and 800 not as a decline but as a transformation. On this view, Roman institutions did not collapse so much as mutate: bishops assumed the functions of municipal magistrates, barbarian kings ruled through Roman law and Roman administrators, and Latin evolved into new languages without ceasing to be a living medium. The framework has the merit of directing attention to religious creativity, to art, and to continuities in everyday life that older narratives ignored. It also rescued the period from the condescension implied by the phrase Dark Ages.

Yet critics argue that the transformation model is too comfortable. Bryan Ward-Perkins and others have pointed to archaeological evidence that seems to resist euphemism: in Britain and parts of the western Mediterranean, the quality and quantity of pottery, coinage, and building declined sharply in the fifth century, and standards of material life fell to levels not seen for centuries. Mass-produced wares that had been available to ordinary households disappeared. Such evidence suggests that a complex economy of long-distance exchange genuinely contracted, and that people living through the change would hardly have described it as a mere transformation. To call this a transition, the critics say, is to let the vocabulary of continuity conceal real loss.

The disagreement is partly empirical and partly a matter of what counts as the thing that ended. If the empire is understood as a political organization with a central tax-collecting state, then it plainly ended in the West, and its disappearance had consequences for those who lived under it. If it is understood as a cultural and religious community, much survived and even flourished. Neither side can simply refute the other with facts, because each selects different facts as the relevant ones. A historian who studies the papyri of Egypt, where administrative continuity under new rulers is abundant, will see a different past than one who excavates a Kent villa abandoned and never reoccupied.

This does not mean that every interpretation is equally good. Some, such as claims of a single cause like lead poisoning or moral decadence, fail because they cannot explain the uneven timing: the eastern empire, subject to the same alleged moral decay, endured for another millennium. A good account must explain regional variation as well as general trends. The most persuasive recent work therefore combines elements of both camps, treating the West's political collapse as swift and its cultural adaptation as gradual, and asking why the same crisis produced such different outcomes in different places.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: survey rival explanations of Rome's fall, show why they persist, and argue that adequate accounts must address regional variation.
options.B: defend the late antiquity model against its critics by showing that archaeological evidence for economic decline is unreliable and incomplete.
options.C: argue that the fall of the Western empire was caused chiefly by fiscal strain, with cultural and religious changes playing only minor roles.
options.D: demonstrate that all interpretations of Rome's fall are equally valid because each reflects the concerns of the period that produced it.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage surveys views, explains the split, and concludes with a regional-variation criterion. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage presents the critics' evidence as serious and does not dismiss it. C) Fiscal strain is mentioned as one twentieth-century explanation, not as the passage's thesis. D) The author explicitly says that not every interpretation is equally good.
questions.trap: Taking the passage's early observation that interpretations reflect their eras as its final claim, overlooking the later rejection of relativism.

questions.stem: The author mentions Gibbon, nineteenth-century nationalists, and twentieth-century scholars in the first paragraph in order to

options.A: suggest that explanations of Rome's fall have repeatedly mirrored the preoccupations of the periods in which they were written.
options.B: show that the study of Rome's fall has progressed steadily, with each generation correcting the errors of the generation before it.
options.C: prove that Christianity, migration, and fiscal strain were each independently sufficient causes of the Western empire's collapse.
options.D: establish that historians who lived through wars and economic crises were better qualified than earlier scholars to judge Rome's decline.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the opening calls Rome a mirror for each age's anxieties and urges caution. Why the others are wrong: B) The paragraph urges caution about the varied narratives rather than praising progress. C) The passage does not claim any factor was sufficient by itself; it later rejects single causes. D) No claim is made that wartime experience gave scholars superior qualifications.
questions.trap: Reading a list of historical views as a progress narrative rather than as evidence of how context shapes interpretation.

questions.stem: Which of the following discoveries would most weaken the critics' use of the pottery evidence from Britain?

options.A: Pottery manufacture in Britain had been declining slowly for more than a century before the empire's political authority ended there.
options.B: Coin finds from fifth-century Britain are rarer than those from the fourth century but are still found at many sites in the region.
options.C: Households in fifth-century Britain shifted to wooden and leather containers made locally, which survive poorly in the archaeological record.
options.D: Pottery production in the eastern Mediterranean continued without interruption throughout the fifth century and long afterward.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) if households switched to perishable local goods, the archaeological disappearance of pottery would not show economic contraction. Why the others are wrong: A) A longer prior decline does not remove the sharp fifth-century drop and might even support contraction. B) Fewer but still present coins would not undermine the claim of decline. D) Eastern continuity is irrelevant to Britain's pottery, and fits the point about regional variation.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence that is merely related to the topic instead of evidence that offers an alternative explanation for the specific data.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward single-cause explanations such as lead poisoning is best described as

options.A: dismissive, because they cannot account for the East's survival under the same alleged conditions that supposedly doomed the West.
options.B: sympathetic, because they offer a simple and elegant unifying principle that the more complicated transformation model cannot provide.
options.C: neutral, because the author considers all claims about the empire's decline equally difficult to test with the surviving evidence.
options.D: cautiously approving, because they could be combined with the transformation model to give a complete account of the cultural changes.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage says single causes fail to explain uneven timing, citing the enduring eastern empire. Why the others are wrong: B) The author criticizes rather than praises these explanations. C) The author explicitly distinguishes better from worse interpretations. D) The passage states that such single causes fail; it does not propose merging them with other views.
questions.trap: Overgeneralizing from the passage's tolerance for multiple perspectives to tolerance for every explanation.

questions.stem: The passage implies that the historian who studies Egyptian papyri and the one who excavates a Kent villa are likely to disagree because

options.A: one of them has misread the evidence, since archaeology and papyrology cannot both produce reliable conclusions about the empire.
options.B: the Egyptian evidence concerns the eastern empire only, so it is irrelevant to any question about the western provinces.
options.C: each works with evidence that makes a different part of the historical record, continuity or abandonment, appear to be typical.
options.D: the papyri show administrative continuity while excavations show economic collapse, so the two cannot be reconciled by any account.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the passage says each side selects different facts as relevant, so evidence base shapes the story. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage does not say either evidence type is unreliable; it says each yields a different past. B) The passage uses the contrast to illustrate differing evidence, not geographic irrelevance. D) The final paragraph says the strongest work combines both camps, so reconciliation is possible.
questions.trap: Concluding that conflicting evidence means one side is wrong, when the passage treats both as accurate but selective.

questions.stem: A study finds that eastern cities kept a functioning tax-collecting administration while western cities lost theirs, and that long-distance trade persisted only where administration persisted. How does this finding relate to the passage?

options.A: It supports the claim that lead poisoning caused the western collapse, since eastern cities were presumably exposed to less lead.
options.B: It supports the combined approach by linking political collapse to economic contraction and helps explain different regional outcomes.
options.C: It undermines the late antiquity model entirely, because that model denies that political institutions had any effect on trade patterns.
options.D: It supports the nineteenth-century migration thesis, because it shows that peoples from the north destroyed western tax systems.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the finding connects political structure to economic contraction and accounts for regional variation, matching the most persuasive recent work. Why the others are wrong: A) Nothing about lead exposure appears in the finding, and the passage rejects that explanation. C) The late antiquity model emphasized continuity, not a denial that institutions affected trade. D) The finding says nothing about migrating peoples as the cause of the administrative loss.
questions.trap: Matching the finding to an explanation named in the passage by surface association rather than by what it actually shows.

passages.passage_text:
Robert Frost is often reported to have said that poetry is what gets lost in translation. Whether or not he said it, the remark expresses a widespread belief that poems are uniquely resistant to being carried from one language into another, since their meaning cannot be separated from the sounds, rhythms, and associations of the words that carry it. If a poem were merely a prose statement dressed in ornament, a translator could extract the statement and re-dress it. But in a poem the dress is part of the body. The pun, the rhyme, the line break, the echo of an older text, all contribute to what the poem says, and none has an exact counterpart in another tongue.

Translators have responded to this predicament in three broad ways. The first, the literalist approach, aims at fidelity to the words, often at the expense of the target language's idiom; the resulting version may read awkwardly, but it allows the reader to see how the original was built. Vladimir Nabokov defended this approach so fiercely that he produced a translation of Pushkin's Eugene Onegin that sacrificed rhyme and meter entirely and loaded the page with footnotes. The second approach, the formalist, tries to reproduce the form: the rhyme scheme, the meter, the stanza. It risks distortion, because rhymes in the new language drag in words the poet never chose. The third, the imitative or free approach, treats the original as an occasion for a new poem, seeking the effect the original had on its first readers rather than its literal content. Ezra Pound's versions of Chinese verse, made without any real knowledge of the language, are the notorious example, and yet they altered English poetry more than most faithful renderings did.

Each strategy implies a theory of what a poem is. The literalist treats it as a document, the formalist as an artifact, the imitator as an event. None captures everything, and it would be a mistake to suppose that a single correct method awaits discovery. A more productive question is what a given translation is for. A version meant to help students read the original line by line has different obligations from one meant to give an English-speaking audience the pleasure of a poem. The same translator may reasonably offer both, as when a bilingual edition places a plain prose crib beside an ambitious verse rendering.

Pessimism about translation also tends to forget that poets themselves are great translators and great borrowers. Much of the English tradition was formed by translations: Chapman's Homer, which Keats praised in a famous sonnet, the King James Bible, and Dryden's Virgil all became part of the language they translated into. In these cases what was lost was less important than what was made. A translation is not a diminished copy but a second work, standing in a relation of dependence and rivalry to the first. Frost's remark, understood this way, is not an indictment but a description of where the translator's labor must go: not into retrieving what cannot be carried over, but into inventing in the new language an equivalent poem that has earned its own life.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the passage's view of translating poetry?

options.A: Translation is better understood as the creation of a second poem for a particular purpose than as the failed transfer of an original.
options.B: Translation is impossible for poetry because form and meaning are inseparable, so any attempt at it should be abandoned by serious readers.
options.C: Translation is best accomplished by the formalist method, which reproduces the original rhyme and meter most accurately in the new language.
options.D: Translation succeeds only when translators know the original language well, as the example of Pound's Chinese verse versions demonstrates.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage concludes that a translation is a second work standing in relation to the first. Why the others are wrong: B) The author rejects pessimism about translation, citing its role in English literature. C) The author says formal reproduction risks distortion and that no single method is correct. D) Pound's versions are cited as influential despite his lack of knowledge, not as a model of success.
questions.trap: Picking the view the passage introduces (poetry resists translation) rather than the view it argues for.

questions.stem: When the author says that in a poem 'the dress is part of the body,' the author means that

options.A: ornamental features of a poem are unimportant, so translators may safely discard them without any loss to the poem's meaning.
options.B: a poem's author usually has a bodily or personal experience in mind, which a translator from another culture cannot fully share.
options.C: the translator must wear the style of the original poet, imitating the manner in which that poet lived as well as wrote.
options.D: a poem's sounds, rhythms, and associations contribute to what it says, so its meaning cannot be separated from its wording.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the sentence follows the claim that prose statements could be re-dressed, and says that form is part of meaning. Why the others are wrong: A) That is the view the metaphor denies. B) The metaphor concerns form and meaning, not the author's bodily experience. C) The metaphor is about words and form, not about the translator's lifestyle.
questions.trap: Reading a metaphor in isolation instead of in light of the preceding sentences that set up its meaning.

questions.stem: The passage uses Ezra Pound's versions of Chinese verse primarily to show that

options.A: a translator's lack of knowledge of the source language is the best qualification for producing a lively and original translation.
options.B: a free rendering can be unfaithful to the original's content and still exert a lasting influence on the target language's poetry.
options.C: the imitative approach is superior to the literalist and formalist approaches in every circumstance in which translators may work.
options.D: English poetry changed more because of translations from Chinese than because of translations from any other language.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the passage calls Pound notorious yet more influential than most faithful renderings. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage calls the example notorious; it does not recommend ignorance. C) The author says no single method is correct, so superiority in every circumstance is not claimed. D) The comparison is with faithful renderings, not with other languages' translations.
questions.trap: Taking an illustrative example as support for a broader, stronger claim than the passage makes.

questions.stem: The author mentions the bilingual edition with a prose crib beside a verse rendering in order to

options.A: argue that the literalist method is ultimately more useful to readers than the imitative method for nearly all poems.
options.B: demonstrate that the verse rendering is merely a decorative addition that depends entirely on the accuracy of the prose version.
options.C: show that bilingual editions are generally preferred by scholars to translations published without the original text alongside.
options.D: illustrate that a single translator may serve two different purposes by offering separate versions suited to each of them.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the example follows the claim that different purposes carry different obligations. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage declines to rank methods. B) The verse rendering is described as ambitious and a work with its own aims. C) The passage makes no claim about scholars' preferences.
questions.trap: Assuming an example shows a preference when the passage only uses it to illustrate coexistence of purposes.

questions.stem: A translator replaces a pun in a Spanish poem with a pun in English that relies on entirely different words but produces a similar comic effect. This approach is most similar to

options.A: the literalist approach, because it preserves the structure of the original so that readers can see how the poem was built.
options.B: the formalist approach, because it keeps the original rhyme scheme and meter intact while changing only the vocabulary.
options.C: none of the approaches described, because puns are said to have no counterpart in another tongue and cannot be translated.
options.D: the imitative approach, because it seeks to reproduce the effect on readers rather than the original's words.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) swapping the words to preserve the effect is how the passage defines imitative translation. Why the others are wrong: A) Literalism would keep the words even at the cost of English idiom. B) The example does not concern rhyme or meter, which formalism targets. C) The passage says puns lack an exact counterpart, but a translator can still seek an equivalent effect.
questions.trap: Matching on the mention of a device (pun, rhyme) rather than on the translator's goal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an assumption on which the author's claim that no single correct method awaits discovery depends?

options.A: Every poem contains a core statement that survives translation in any method, so the methods differ only in their manner of presenting it.
options.B: Readers who cannot read the original will always judge a translation by its literal accuracy rather than by its poetic effect in English.
options.C: Translators who adopt one method consistently produce better results than translators who switch among methods from one poem to the next.
options.D: Translations serve different readers and aims, and a method suited to one aim may be poorly suited to another.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the author ties method to what the translation is for, so differing aims is the premise. Why the others are wrong: A) The author denies that a poem is a prose statement in ornament. B) The passage says audiences may want pleasure, not literal accuracy. C) The passage notes that one translator may reasonably offer both versions.
questions.trap: Selecting a claim that sounds related to translation instead of one needed by the specific argument.

passages.passage_text:
When Kandinsky painted what is often called the first abstract watercolor around 1910, he did not think he was abandoning meaning; he believed he was releasing it. Colors and shapes, he argued, act directly on the soul, as musical tones do, without needing to depict anything. The comparison with music was crucial to early abstractionists, since music had long been admired as the art that said what it said without representing the world. If a symphony needed no picture of a thunderstorm to move its audience, a canvas might need no landscape. Abstraction, on this account, is not an absence of subject matter but a discovery of a different kind of subject: the inner life, rendered in pure form.

A second tradition understood abstraction less as expression than as inquiry. Mondrian, moving through a series of increasingly stripped-down paintings of a tree, arrived at a grid of black lines and primary colors that he regarded as the visual structure underlying all appearances. His project resembled a philosophical reduction: remove the accidental, and the essential is left. Later, critics such as Clement Greenberg gave this impulse a different rationale. For Greenberg, modernist painting advanced by discarding everything that was not unique to the medium itself, such as illusionistic depth and storytelling, until it concentrated on the flat surface and the arrangement of pigment upon it. Abstraction was the logical end point of painting's attempt to know its own nature.

Skeptics have long objected that abstract painting is easy to fake and impossible to judge. If a canvas of splashed paint carries no recognizable skill in drawing, how can one distinguish achievement from accident? The objection has some force against the careless claim that abstract works can mean anything the viewer wants. But it overlooks the fact that abstract painters work under severe constraints of their own. Without a represented object to supply coherence, the painter must make the relations of color, weight, and edge do all the work, and the result either holds together or visibly fails. Viewers often detect the difference quickly, even when they cannot explain it, in the way listeners hear a wrong note without being trained musicians. Jackson Pollock's drip paintings, which looked random to many contemporaries, display on close study a controlled density and rhythm that imitators have rarely matched.

There remains a more sociological doubt. Abstraction, some historians point out, flourished in the postwar United States partly because institutions found it congenial: it was apolitical, it seemed to embody individual freedom, and it could be exhibited abroad as a contrast to officially mandated realism elsewhere. Those who hold this view do not claim the paintings were insincere. Their point is that the meaning of an artwork is not exhausted by the intentions of its maker, for institutions, critics, and governments confer meanings of their own. What began as a spiritual or analytic quest could thus become an emblem of a political ideal. That an art form may serve purposes its practitioners never foresaw is no reason to deny it value; it is, rather, a reminder that painting, like every human activity, exists in a world that uses it.

questions.stem: The main point of the passage is that

options.A: abstract painting is the highest form of art because it expresses the inner life without relying on the limits of representation.
options.B: abstract painting has several justifications, resists the charge of arbitrariness, and acquires meanings its makers never intended.
options.C: abstract painting flourished in the postwar United States only because institutions promoted it for political purposes they favored.
options.D: abstract painting is widely misunderstood because viewers lack the training to see the technical skill that its practitioners possess.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the passage covers expressive and analytic rationales, replies to skeptics, and the sociological point. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage never ranks abstraction as the highest art form. C) The historians do not claim the paintings were insincere or only political, and the passage says institutions merely conferred additional meanings. D) The passage says viewers often detect quality without training.
questions.trap: Selecting the claim from one section of the passage as if it were the claim of the whole passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the views of Kandinsky and Greenberg differ in that

options.A: Kandinsky saw abstraction as expressing inner life directly, whereas Greenberg saw it as painting's concentration on what is unique to its medium.
options.B: Kandinsky regarded abstraction as an inquiry into hidden structure, whereas Greenberg regarded it as a rejection of all rules of composition.
options.C: Kandinsky wished to eliminate emotion from painting, whereas Greenberg wished to restore emotion by returning to illusionistic depth and storytelling.
options.D: Kandinsky defended abstraction by analogy with music, whereas Greenberg defended it by analogy with philosophical reduction of experience.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage ties Kandinsky to the soul and music analogy, and Greenberg to the medium's self-knowledge. Why the others are wrong: B) The structural inquiry belongs to Mondrian, and Greenberg valued the medium's own properties, not lawlessness. C) Kandinsky valued emotion, and Greenberg wanted to discard illusionistic depth. D) The philosophical reduction is attributed to Mondrian, not Greenberg.
questions.trap: Swapping the attributions of the rationales among the painters and critics named in the passage.

questions.stem: The author responds to the skeptics' charge that abstract painting cannot be judged by arguing that

options.A: abstract painters face their own constraints, since color and form relations must alone hold the work together.
options.B: abstract painting is judged by the same standards as representational painting, such as the skill of drawing and accuracy of likeness.
options.C: the judgments of trained critics are the only reliable way of telling accomplished abstract works from works produced by accident.
options.D: viewers who dislike abstract works usually change their opinions after they learn about the intentions and biographies of the painters.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage says the work either holds together or visibly fails, a detectable difference. Why the others are wrong: B) The skeptics' point was that such skill is absent; the author does not reply by asserting it. C) The author says untrained viewers can detect differences, like hearing a wrong note. D) Nothing in the passage addresses changes in viewers' opinions.
questions.trap: Offering a reply that concedes the skeptics' premise rather than answering it.

questions.stem: The comparison to listeners who hear a wrong note without musical training functions to

options.A: suggest that abstract painting is a form of music and should be judged exclusively by the standards of musical criticism.
options.B: illustrate Kandinsky's claim that colors act on the soul in the same way that musical tones do without depicting anything.
options.C: support the claim that viewers can often perceive a difference in quality without being able to explain it.
options.D: argue that only specialists can reliably tell a successful abstract painting from a failed one, as in the case of music.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the analogy follows the claim that viewers detect the difference quickly without explaining it. Why the others are wrong: A) The analogy concerns perception of quality, not a merger of the arts. B) That earlier music comparison concerned expression, not the detection of quality. D) The analogy says training is not needed.
questions.trap: Confusing two separate uses of music analogies in the passage.

questions.stem: The historians mentioned in the last paragraph would most likely agree with which of the following?

options.A: An artwork can come to carry significance, such as political symbolism, that its creator did not intend and never anticipated.
options.B: Abstract painters in the postwar United States insincerely adopted their style because they knew that institutions would reward it.
options.C: An artwork's meaning is determined entirely by the response of critics, governments, and institutions rather than by its maker.
options.D: Abstraction should be regarded as less valuable than realist painting because it served political ends it was not meant to serve.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage says meaning is not exhausted by intentions and that institutions confer meanings. Why the others are wrong: B) The historians explicitly do not claim the paintings were insincere. C) The claim is that meaning is not exhausted by intent, not that it is determined solely by others. D) The author says that serving unforeseen purposes is no reason to deny value.
questions.trap: Choosing an extreme restatement (entirely determined) of a moderate claim (not exhausted).

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most undermine the author's response to the skeptics?

options.A: Viewers with art training, shown pairs of Pollock paintings and skilled imitations, preferred the imitations about half of the time they were tested.
options.B: Viewers with no art training, shown pairs of Pollock paintings and random splatters, identified the genuine Pollocks no more often than chance would predict.
options.C: Viewers shown abstract paintings reported that they found the works emotionally moving but could not explain their reactions in words.
options.D: Viewers shown a series of Mondrian grids and the same grids with lines shifted preferred the originals only when they knew the artist.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) chance-level discrimination by untrained viewers contradicts the claim that the difference between success and failure is often detected quickly. Why the others are wrong: A) Trained viewers' preferences do not test the claim about untrained detection, and imitation differs from random splatters. C) Being moved without being able to explain is exactly what the author describes. D) That result is about knowledge of the artist and Mondrian, not about untrained detection of quality; it does not directly address Pollock versus randomness.
questions.trap: Selecting a result about experts or emotion when the author's claim concerned untrained viewers' detection of quality.

passages.passage_text:
In 1966, the Beach Boys' Pet Sounds and then the Beatles' Revolver made it clear that the recording studio had ceased to be a place where performances were merely captured. Tape loops, varied playback speeds, and layered overdubs produced sounds that no group of musicians could have played together in a room. The producer and theorist Brian Eno later gave this development its most quoted formulation, describing the studio as a compositional tool, an instrument in its own right, that could be played as a guitar is played. The claim is more than a metaphor, and it explains why bands of this period began to book studio time as they once booked concert halls. A guitarist's craft consists in exploiting the physical properties of strings, wood, and amplification; a studio artist exploits the properties of tape saturation, reverberation chambers, and microphone placement, and develops comparable skill in doing so.

The idea unsettles an older view of recording as a window onto a performance. According to that view, the best recording is the most transparent one, and engineering ought to disappear, preserving as faithfully as possible an event that occurred in a particular hall. Classical labels long worked under this ideal, sending engineers to hide their equipment and keep it out of the artists' sight, and live-in-concert albums still invoke it. Yet even the transparent recording involves choices. Where the microphones are placed, how many are used, and whether the room's reverberation is included alter the sound dramatically, and a listener at home hears something no member of the audience ever heard. The window, on inspection, is a painted window.

If the studio is an instrument, then questions about authorship become tangled. Who plays it? Phil Spector, with his dense wall of sound, was credited as the author of records that others sang and played. George Martin shaped the Beatles' arrangements with scoring and tape editing. Later, hip-hop producers built entire tracks from fragments of earlier recordings, treating the turntable and sampler as instruments. In each case the person at the console contributes something that cannot be traced to any musician's hands. Some critics respond by narrowing the idea of musical authorship to composition and performance, and treating engineering as craft service. This distinction seems increasingly arbitrary, since a record's most identifiable feature, its sound, is often precisely what the engineer and producer have made.

There is also a cost to the studio as instrument. Because editing allows any imperfection to be corrected, listeners may come to expect a polish that live musicians cannot supply, and performers sometimes find themselves judged against recordings that were themselves composites. Pitch correction software, which can adjust a singer's intonation note by note, has made this concern more urgent. Some artists have responded by deliberately preserving flaws, recording live to tape in one take as a statement of authenticity. Even this gesture, however, depends on the studio's resources: the choice of one take is a decision about how the recording will sound, and an act of production like any other. The studio cannot be switched off; it can only be used with more or less visible intention.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.A: The recording studio has been harmful to music because editing tools have led listeners to expect a polish that live performers cannot give.
options.B: The recording studio functions as an instrument that shapes the sound of music, which complicates ideas about authorship and authenticity.
options.C: The recording studio should be used only to capture live performances transparently, as classical labels have long attempted to do.
options.D: The recording studio became important only after 1966, when tape techniques first allowed producers to credit themselves as authors.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the passage argues the studio is an instrument and traces its consequences for authorship and authenticity. Why the others are wrong: A) The cost of polish is discussed but is only one part of the argument. C) The transparency ideal is the view the passage unsettles. D) The passage dates one development to 1966 but does not say the studio only then became important or that credit was the aim.
questions.trap: Selecting a detail from one paragraph as the passage's main idea.

questions.stem: When the author calls the transparent recording 'a painted window,' the author means that

options.A: recordings made to appear faithful are in fact dishonest because they conceal the actual identity of the musicians performing.
options.B: listeners typically admire the decoration of a recording more than the performance that the recording is meant to preserve.
options.C: even recordings that aim to disappear involve choices about microphones and room sound that shape what the listener hears.
options.D: classical recordings are inferior to studio-constructed albums because they are limited by the acoustics of a single hall.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the author says microphone placement and reverberation alter the sound so the listener hears what no audience member heard. Why the others are wrong: A) The point concerns technical choices, not the musicians' identity. B) The metaphor says nothing about admiration for decoration over performance. D) The author does not rank classical recordings as inferior.
questions.trap: Reading the metaphor as a moral charge of dishonesty rather than a point about unavoidable mediation.

questions.stem: The author discusses Spector, Martin, and hip-hop producers in order to

options.A: show that producers and engineers contribute to records in ways that cannot be attributed to the hands of any performing musician.
options.B: prove that the best recordings result from having a producer who is also the principal performer and composer of the music.
options.C: argue that sampling and tape editing have no value unless they are used to reproduce earlier performances exactly.
options.D: illustrate how the older view of recording as a window onto performance was gradually perfected by more skilled engineers.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage states that in each case the person at the console contributes something untraceable to the musicians. Why the others are wrong: B) Spector and Martin are described as shaping records others played; they are not described as performers. C) Hip-hop producers are said to build new tracks from fragments, not reproduce them. D) These cases are offered as challenges to, not perfections of, the window view.
questions.trap: Assuming that illustrations of producers' roles imply that producers should also be the performers.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward recording live to tape in a single take as a statement of authenticity is best described as

options.A: fully supportive, because the gesture restores the performers' control over the sound that the studio had previously taken away.
options.B: scornful, because the gesture is dishonest in pretending that engineers and producers played no part in the resulting record.
options.C: indifferent, because the author regards all questions of authenticity as irrelevant to the use of the studio as an instrument.
options.D: appreciative but unpersuaded, since the choice is itself a production decision made with the studio's resources.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the passage says the gesture still depends on the studio and is an act of production like any other. Why the others are wrong: A) The author denies that the gesture escapes the studio's influence. B) The tone is measured; the author does not accuse artists of dishonesty. C) The author discusses authenticity at length and treats it as a real concern.
questions.trap: Taking a nuanced evaluation to be wholly positive or wholly negative.

questions.stem: A photographer chooses a lens, exposure, and darkroom technique to produce an image that no unaided eye would see. The author would most likely regard this as

options.A: a contrast with the studio artist's work, since photographers merely record scenes while studio artists compose entirely new sounds.
options.B: evidence that photography is superior to recording, because photographers receive credit for all the choices made in their art.
options.C: irrelevant to the passage, because the argument concerns only music and cannot be extended to any other art form.
options.D: analogous to the studio artist's work, since both shape the final product through the properties of the medium's equipment.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the passage's argument about microphone placement and tape properties parallels these technical choices shaping the result. Why the others are wrong: A) The author denies that engineering is mere recording; so the contrast fails. B) The passage makes no comparison of credit among arts. C) The argument is about shaping through instruments, so it does extend by analogy.
questions.trap: Rejecting a fitting analogy because it comes from a different domain.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that engineers and producers make a record's most identifiable feature, its sound?

options.A: Listeners asked to rate records preferred those with more elaborate production when the underlying songs were of equal quality.
options.B: Musicians asked to describe their own albums said that producers had substantial influence over the sounds heard on the recordings.
options.C: Listeners asked to identify famous records relied overwhelmingly on melody and lyrics rather than on production textures.
options.D: Listeners shown pitch-corrected and uncorrected versions of the same vocal performance often could not tell which version was which.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) if identification rests on melody and lyrics rather than sonic texture, the sound is not what makes a record most identifiable. Why the others are wrong: A) Preference for elaborate production would suggest production matters to listeners. B) Musicians' reports of producer influence would support the claim. D) Failure to hear pitch correction concerns one effect and does not show that the sound is not identifiable.
questions.trap: Choosing a result that bears on production in general rather than on what makes records identifiable.

passages.passage_text:
Marcel Mauss's 1925 essay on the gift began from a puzzle. In many societies he surveyed, goods were exchanged not through markets but through elaborate cycles of giving, receiving, and reciprocating, and yet these transfers were neither free nor purely voluntary. A gift, Mauss argued, creates an obligation to return something, and the sense of obligation is as binding as a contract. The Trobriand Islanders' kula, in which shell necklaces and armbands circulate in opposite directions among islands for years, was his central example. Participants did not keep the valuables; honor came from holding one briefly and passing it on. Reciprocity here is not haggling; to calculate the return too openly would be an insult to the partner. Mauss concluded that the gift is a total social phenomenon, simultaneously economic, religious, legal, and moral.

Modern readers frequently take from Mauss the thought that there is no such thing as a pure gift. If a gift places the recipient in debt, then every gift contains a hidden transaction. Jacques Derrida pressed this to a paradoxical conclusion: a true gift would have to be unrecognized by both the giver, who would gain no credit, and the receiver, who would feel no debt, but then it would not be a gift at all. The argument is ingenious, but it may mistake a feature of gifts for a flaw. That gifts create relationships is precisely what distinguishes them from sales. A purchase ends the connection between buyer and seller, since the goods change hands and the account is settled. A gift, by leaving the account open, keeps the parties bound to each other.

This difference explains why attempts to convert gifts into money often offend. In a well-known study of day care centers in Haifa, researchers introduced a fine for parents who arrived late to collect their children. Lateness increased rather than declined, and it remained high even after the fine was removed. One interpretation is that the fine altered the nature of the relationship: lateness, once a favor requiring apology, became a service with a posted price. Where teachers had relied on parents' sense of obligation, the fine replaced obligation with payment, and the moral cost of being late vanished. The case is commonly cited in support of the claim that market incentives can crowd out social norms, though critics note that it was a single study in a small number of centers.

Gift exchange is not confined to traditional societies. Blood donation, which in many countries relies on unpaid volunteers, was the subject of Richard Titmuss's argument that a system of voluntary donation produces a safer supply than payment and also expresses social solidarity. Open-source software, in which programmers contribute code that others may use freely, shows a similar logic. Contributors gain reputation and belonging, which are not prices but do function as returns. Such examples suggest that the gift and the market are not alternatives dividing the world into two zones; they are different ways of organizing the same activities, with different effects on how people regard one another, and societies choose, often unconsciously, between them.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.A: explain Mauss's idea of the gift and argue that gifts and markets are different ways of organizing similar activities.
options.B: refute Mauss's claim that gifts create obligations by showing that modern gift-giving is voluntary and disinterested.
options.C: argue that market incentives should never be applied to activities such as childcare, blood donation, or open-source programming.
options.D: defend Derrida's argument that gifts are impossible because every apparently generous act contains a concealed transaction.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage moves from Mauss to consequences and concludes that gift and market are different organizations of activity. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage supports, rather than refutes, the idea that gifts bind. C) The author cites the Haifa case cautiously and does not make an absolute claim. D) The author says Derrida's argument mistakes a feature of gifts for a flaw.
questions.trap: Treating a position the author discusses (Derrida's) as the author's own.

questions.stem: The author says that Derrida 'may mistake a feature of gifts for a flaw' because

options.A: Derrida failed to notice that recipients of gifts normally feel no sense of debt to the giver of the gift.
options.B: Derrida overlooked the fact that gifts are always exchanged in cycles, as in the kula, across several different islands.
options.C: creating a continuing relationship through obligation is what distinguishes a gift from a sale, so it is not a defect.
options.D: Derrida wrongly assumed that the giver of a gift gains no reputation or credit from the giving of the gift.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the passage contrasts open accounts in gifts with settled accounts in purchases. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage accepts that gifts create debt. B) The kula example does not address Derrida's point about purity. D) Derrida's own argument said the giver would gain no credit in a true gift; that is not what the author criticizes.
questions.trap: Mixing up Derrida's premises with the author's objection to his conclusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the crowding-out interpretation of the Haifa day care study?

options.A: Parents at the centers reported that they felt guilty about arriving late both before and after the fine was introduced.
options.B: Lateness remained elevated after the fine was removed, even though teachers reminded parents that lateness imposed costs on staff.
options.C: Similar fines in other countries, in settings such as libraries, reduced the frequency of overdue returns by borrowers.
options.D: When the fine was introduced, centers also extended their official closing time, and parents read the fine as payment for the extra hours.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) a change in the closing time offers a different explanation for the rise in lateness, independent of any moral shift. Why the others are wrong: A) Guilt both before and after is not clearly inconsistent with the interpretation, and could even support it. B) Persisting lateness after removal fits the idea that norms were damaged. C) Results in other settings do not address what happened in the Haifa centers.
questions.trap: Choosing an outside case instead of a confound within the study itself.

questions.stem: The discussion of open-source software mainly serves to

options.A: demonstrate that programmers who contribute code receive no benefit from their contributions beyond the satisfaction of giving.
options.B: prove that voluntary contribution always produces higher-quality products than the commercial software developed by firms.
options.C: show that gift logic operates in modern settings and that returns to giving need not take the form of prices.
options.D: illustrate the argument that Trobriand kula exchange and open-source programming rely on the same specific set of rules.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the passage says contributors gain reputation and belonging, which function as returns but are not prices. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says that contributors do gain reputation and belonging. B) The passage compares blood donation safety with payment, but it does not make a general quality claim about software. D) The parallel is one of logic, not of identical rules.
questions.trap: Over-reading a parallel as an identity or as a claim about quality.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of the passage's idea that the same activity can be organized as a gift or as a market?

options.A: A shopkeeper selling goods at a discount to a customer who happens to be a close friend of the family.
options.B: A neighbor who borrows tools and keeps them permanently, which the owner regards as an unfair taking of property.
options.C: A museum that charges admission on most days but waives the entrance fee for all visitors on the first Sunday of each month.
options.D: Care for an aging parent given by family out of obligation versus by a paid nursing agency under contract.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the same activity, caring for a parent, can be organized by obligation or payment, with differing effects on relationships. Why the others are wrong: A) This is a sale with a personal discount, not a different organization of the same activity. B) This is a dispute over taking property, not an alternative organization of one activity. C) A fee waiver is a pricing practice and does not shift the relationship from market to gift.
questions.trap: Choosing an example involving money and friendship by surface features rather than the underlying parallel.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a purchase differs from a gift in that a purchase

options.A: involves no obligation of any kind, whereas a gift creates obligations that are binding only in traditional societies.
options.B: requires equal value to change hands, whereas a gift requires only that the recipient accept the thing offered.
options.C: depends on the legal system for enforcement, whereas a gift depends solely on the private feelings of the giver.
options.D: settles the account between the parties and ends their connection, whereas a gift leaves the account open.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the passage states that goods change hands and the account is settled in a purchase. Why the others are wrong: A) Purchases have obligations like payment, and the passage says obligations in gifts exist in modern settings too. B) The passage does not claim a purchase needs equal value or that a gift needs only acceptance. C) The passage says gift obligations are as binding as contract, not merely private feeling.
questions.trap: Attributing to the passage a contrast it does not draw.

passages.passage_text:
Defenders of federalism often begin with an argument about information: governments close to the people know local conditions better than a distant capital can. Madison's Federalist No. 10 gave the idea a different, more surprising turn. Rather than praising small units for their cohesion, he argued that a large republic is safer than a small one against the dangers of faction, since in an extended territory many interests will compete and no single one is likely to dominate. Both arguments treat the division of authority as a tool for managing human limitations rather than as a good in itself. The federal structure of the United States has been defended ever since on both grounds: as a way of keeping government responsive and as a way of preventing any group from capturing all its power at once.

A third argument, associated with Justice Brandeis's remark that a state may serve as a laboratory of democracy, emphasizes experimentation. Different jurisdictions may try different policies, and others can observe the results at little cost. Welfare reform, minimum wage increases, and the legalization of various activities have each spread from a few states to many. The argument assumes, however, that lessons transfer: that a policy that succeeds in one state would succeed in another. Where populations, industries, and institutions differ greatly, the experiment may prove nothing, and the confidence of reformers who cite a neighbor's success may be misplaced.

Critics of federalism have pointed to costs that its defenders tend to underplay. The most serious is historical: in the United States, the doctrine of states' rights was invoked to defend slavery and later to resist civil rights legislation, and the protection of local self-government in these cases meant the protection of local oppression. A second cost is competition among jurisdictions. If states compete for businesses by lowering taxes or relaxing regulations, the result may be a race to the bottom in which every state offers less protection to its citizens than any would choose on its own. Economists remain divided about how often such races actually occur, since businesses weigh many factors besides regulation, but the possibility has been used to justify national standards in areas such as environmental protection.

The attempt to decide in the abstract whether federalism is good is therefore probably misguided. The relevant question is which functions are better assigned to which level. Matters whose effects stay within a locality, such as the layout of streets or the management of a school, seem suited to local control. Matters whose effects spill across borders, such as air pollution or the regulation of interstate commerce, seem to require a wider authority. Matters involving basic rights seem to demand a uniform floor that no locality may breach. Even this division invites disagreement, for the classification of any given issue is often itself a contested political question. Federalism, in the end, is less a settled doctrine than a continuing negotiation about where to draw lines, with the lines moving as the circumstances and the stakes change.

questions.stem: The passage as a whole is best described as

options.A: a defense of federalism based on the claim that local governments always know local conditions better than any distant national authority could.
options.B: a historical account of how the doctrine of states' rights was used to resist civil rights legislation in the United States.
options.C: an evaluation of arguments for and against federalism that ends by recasting the issue as one of assigning functions to levels of government.
options.D: an argument that national standards should replace state authority in matters such as environmental protection and interstate commerce.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the passage reviews defenses and criticisms and ends with a function-assignment framing. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage lists problems with that argument and does not say it holds always. B) That history is one criticism, not the passage's overall subject. D) The passage says some matters suit local control, so replacement is not its thesis.
questions.trap: Choosing one part of the passage as its overall purpose.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Madison's argument in Federalist No. 10 is surprising because it

options.A: claims that governments close to the people have better information, whereas one might expect distant governments to have more resources.
options.B: claims that states may serve as laboratories of democracy, whereas one might expect national governments to have more experience.
options.C: claims that states' rights protect local self-government, whereas one might expect them to endanger the rights of minorities.
options.D: claims that a large republic is safer than a small one against faction, whereas one might expect small units to be more cohesive and safer.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the passage says Madison argued that many competing interests in a large territory prevent domination. Why the others are wrong: A) The information argument is the opening one and not Madison's turn. B) The laboratory remark is attributed to Brandeis. C) The states' rights issue belongs to the critics' section.
questions.trap: Attributing arguments to the wrong person among those named in the passage.

questions.stem: The laboratory-of-democracy argument, as presented in the passage, assumes that

options.A: state governments always choose policies that are better than those which would be selected by the national government.
options.B: a policy that works in one jurisdiction would also work in another, so observers can learn from the neighboring experiment.
options.C: policy experiments should be limited to the legalization of activities that are currently prohibited in most jurisdictions.
options.D: citizens of different states hold the same preferences about taxes and regulation, which makes competition unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the passage says the argument assumes lessons transfer. Why the others are wrong: A) No assumption about states' superiority is stated. C) The passage lists welfare reform and minimum wages too, so no such limit exists. D) The assumption concerns transfer of results, not preferences.
questions.trap: Selecting a plausible-sounding premise not stated or needed in the passage.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations is most clearly a function that the author would assign to a wider authority?

options.A: A town decides how wide its streets should be and where to place its crosswalks near the schools.
options.B: A school district chooses between two reading curricula for its elementary schools on the basis of local test results.
options.C: A factory in an upstream state discharges waste into a river, harming the water supply of a downstream state.
options.D: A county decides on the hours during which its public library will be open on weekends throughout the year.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) effects that spill across borders, such as pollution, require a wider authority. Why the others are wrong: A) Street layout is a local matter in the passage. B) School management is named as suited to local control. D) Library hours are a purely local matter whose effects stay within the community.
questions.trap: Choosing examples that share the setting of the passage's local examples rather than its spillover criterion.

questions.stem: The author's view on whether federalism can be judged good or bad in the abstract is that

options.A: the question has a clear answer, since the historical costs of federalism clearly outweigh the benefits that its defenders cite.
options.B: the question is poorly posed, because the real issue is which functions are better assigned to which level of government.
options.C: the question has a clear answer, since the three standard defenses of federalism are sufficient to establish its general value.
options.D: the question cannot be answered because economists disagree about whether races to the bottom actually occur among states.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the passage calls abstract judgment misguided and recasts the question in terms of assigning functions. Why the others are wrong: A) The author does not weigh the totals in that way. C) The author does not claim the defenses suffice. D) The economists' disagreement is a side point and not the reason the question is misguided.
questions.trap: Taking an unresolved empirical dispute as the author's reason for a conceptual objection.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most weaken the race-to-the-bottom worry described in the passage?

options.A: Firms choose locations mostly for workforce skills and nearness to customers, and rarely change those choices over regulatory differences.
options.B: States that lowered business taxes subsequently reported that their revenue available for schools and road repair was smaller than before.
options.C: States with stricter environmental rules were more likely to be sued by firms than states with looser rules over the same period, mostly over permit disputes.
options.D: Citizens of states with weaker protections reported that they would prefer stronger protections if the national government required them.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) if regulations rarely affect firms' location, states have little incentive to compete by relaxing them. Why the others are wrong: B) Reduced revenue would support concern about harms from competing on taxes. C) Lawsuits do not address whether states relax rules to attract firms. D) Citizen preference for stronger protection fits the worry that states provide less than residents would choose.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence about consequences of competition rather than evidence about whether the competition occurs.

passages.passage_text:
Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) proposed that science does not advance by the steady accumulation of facts. Instead, long periods of normal science, in which researchers solve puzzles within a shared framework, are punctuated by revolutions in which the framework itself is replaced. A paradigm, in Kuhn's usage, is not merely a theory but a package of exemplary achievements, methods, and assumptions that tells practitioners which questions are worth asking and what counts as an answer. Anomalies, results that the paradigm cannot absorb, accumulate until a crisis arises and a rival framework gains adherents. The transition is not simply a matter of weighing evidence, Kuhn claimed, because the competing paradigms disagree about what the evidence is.

This last claim, the incommensurability of paradigms, provoked the fiercest criticism. If scientists on opposite sides of a revolution cannot even agree on the meaning of terms such as mass or planet, then it seems that they cannot rationally persuade one another, and the choice between theories would resemble a religious conversion. Critics such as Karl Popper and Imre Lakatos worried that this made science irrational. Kuhn later insisted he had been misread: he held that theory choice involves shared values such as accuracy, consistency, and fruitfulness, which guide scientists even when they cannot be applied as an algorithm. Reasonable scientists may weigh the values differently, and for that reason early disagreement during a transition is rational rather than a symptom of mass irrationality.

Historians of science have also challenged the neatness of Kuhn's picture. The Copernican revolution, his favorite example, took more than a century, and Copernicus's own system used epicycles and was hardly simpler or more accurate than Ptolemy's. No single moment divides the old from the new. In some fields, such as geology, the acceptance of plate tectonics in the 1960s resembled a revolution, with a long-resisted hypothesis rapidly winning over a field after new evidence from the ocean floor. In others, such as the development of molecular biology, change came through a series of overlapping refinements with no clear crisis. It may be that revolution describes the extreme end of a continuum, and that much scientific change is intermediate.

Whatever its limitations, Kuhn's account altered how scientists and the public think about science. It undermined the image of the scientist as a lone reasoner confronting nature without presuppositions, and it drew attention to the role of education, community, and institutions in sustaining a research tradition. It also gave a name to a familiar experience: that younger researchers are often quicker than their elders to adopt a new framework. That observation can be abused, as when fringe thinkers cite Kuhn to claim that their rejection by the mainstream proves they are the next revolutionaries. But rejection by one's peers is not evidence of being right. Kuhn himself would have insisted that the vast majority of challenges to a paradigm fail, and that a paradigm's resistance to change, though sometimes a vice, is also what allows normal science to make steady progress.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?

options.A: Kuhn's account of scientific revolutions has been influential, criticized, and refined, yet remains useful for understanding scientific change.
options.B: Kuhn showed that scientific theories are chosen by irrational conversion, which proves that science has no more authority than other beliefs.
options.C: Kuhn's account has been entirely discredited by historians, who have shown that scientific change always proceeds through gradual refinement.
options.D: Kuhn argued that younger scientists are always right about new frameworks, so that established researchers should defer to them.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage presents the theory, criticisms, historians' complications, and lasting influence. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage reports that Kuhn insisted theory choice involves shared values. C) The passage says some fields did see revolutions, such as geology. D) The passage says younger researchers are quicker to adopt, not that they are always right.
questions.trap: Selecting an extreme conclusion that the passage itself contradicts.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a paradigm is best understood as

options.A: a single scientific theory that has been confirmed by enough evidence to be accepted by all of the members of a research community.
options.B: a package of exemplary achievements, methods, and assumptions that guides which questions practitioners ask and what counts as an answer.
options.C: a set of anomalies that a research community has agreed to ignore until a rival framework gains more adherents.
options.D: an institutional arrangement for educating young scientists, with textbooks, laboratories, and journals all organized around one particular discipline.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the passage defines it as more than a theory, a package of achievements, methods, and assumptions. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says it is not merely a theory. C) Anomalies are what paradigms cannot absorb, not what they define. D) Education is mentioned as an influence in the last paragraph, not as the definition.
questions.trap: Reducing a defined term to its most familiar sense.

questions.stem: Critics worried that incommensurability made science irrational because it implied that

options.A: scientists would never abandon a paradigm no matter how many anomalies accumulated, since each paradigm defines its own evidence.
options.B: scientists in normal science could not solve puzzles, since the puzzles of a paradigm would not be acknowledged by its practitioners.
